summary: Amur cork tree is a tree up to 40 feet tall with corky, grey, furrowed bark and bright yellow inner bark. Its leaves have 5 to 11 leaflets that smell of citrus or disinfectant when crushed. Its shade can keep native trees, shrubs and wildflowers from growing, it releases chemicals into the soil that harm native plants and soil microorganisms, and its fruit is less nutritious for birds than native fruit. It tolerates sun or deep shade, drought, flooding and pollution, so it does well in cities.
history: Amur cork tree is native to East Asia. It was brought to the United States in the mid-1800s as a landscape tree. Female trees produce thousands of seeds, which birds spread.
seasons: Male and female flowers grow on separate trees. Female trees bloom with clusters of small green flowers in late spring, which become drooping clusters of small, round, black fruit in mid-fall. The fruit stays on the trees through the winter.

handling.text: Managers remove female trees first to cut seed production. Seedlings and saplings can be hand-pulled; trees that are cut down will resprout unless the stump is treated, so control takes several years.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
